Field notes on sourdough hydration

Hydration is the weight of water in a dough divided by the weight of flour, written as a percentage. A loaf made with 1,000 grams of flour and 750 grams of water is a 75 percent dough. The number is simple; what it does to the bread is not, because flour does not absorb water the same way from one bag to the next.

Over twelve bakes we kept the starter, the salt and the oven the same and moved only the water. At 65 percent the dough was easy to shape and the crumb was tight and even. At 75 percent the dough spread on the bench, but the loaf rose higher in the oven and the crumb opened up. At 85 percent the dough needed a series of folds over two hours before it would hold any shape at all.

What changed between bakes

  • Whole wheat flour drank about five points more water than white flour before the dough felt the same.
  • A longer cold proof made the wetter doughs easier to score.
  • Fresh flour needed less water than flour from a bag that had been open for a month.

The practical rule we ended with: start at 70 percent with a new flour, hold back a tenth of the water, and add it during the first set of folds only if the dough feels stiff. See the flour notes for the full table of weights and times.

None of this needs special equipment. A kitchen scale that reads single grams, a bowl with straight sides so you can see the rise, and a notebook are enough to learn what your own flour wants.
